launchFacilities: Currently, the Guiana Space Center is the only launch facility in Europe to have conducted successful orbital launches. The Andøya Spaceport and Esrange Space Center were formally inaugurated in 2023 but have yet to successful launch an asset into orbit. Andøya attempted a first launch in November 2025 with Isar Aerospace and is aiming to conduct a second test launch in Q2 2026,.4 Esrange is also looking to secure its first test launch with Firefly Aerospace, marking the first US launch in a foreign country. The Center has also secured a deal with the Korean company Perigee Aerospace to launch satellites from Kiruna using their Blue Whale 1 microlauncher.5 The majority of European planned facilities also cater to small or microlaunchers, which limits the overall scope of European launch capacity.

As mentioned previously, New European launch facilities are focusing on LEO launches, primarily to SSO and Polar orbits due to their higher latitudes. Therefore, launch capabilities remain quite limited in their orbital focus, as well as the specific launchers they cater to. Small and microlaunchers are at the forefront of these initiatives as Europe is also promoting a more multifaceted launch environment with new start-ups and emerging companies racing to ensure their first launches from European sites.

Launch sites and infrastructure used for recovery of launch vehicles. European launch capabilities are primarily concentrated in the Guiana Space Center located in the French department of Guiana in South America. Emerging actors such as the Andøya Spaceport (Norway) and Esrange Space Center (Sweden) are seeking to diversify existing efforts in European launch capacity. However, these launch centres focus on specific orbital launches to LEO and polar orbits, in part, due to their high latitudes. Additional efforts are being developed across the continent in Denmark, Portugal, Spain and the UK among others. The UK currently leads with the most registered spaceport initiatives, with five projects across the country. However, the main contender in the UK launch race is the SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland. Offshore capabilities are also in development through the EuroSpaceport and North Sea Launch platform initiatives, yet these remain still in the inception phase, therefore these platforms are not analysed in detail the frame of this study.

testCentres: Testing centres form a critical part of Europe’s access to space infrastructure, because they provide the facilities required to develop, validate, qualify, and de-risk propulsion systems and launch hardware before flight. Europe’s testing landscape is centred particularly, but not exclusively, on propulsion spanning liquid, solid, cryogenic, and emerging green systems, for launchers. This landscape includes long-established national research centres such as DLR Lampoldshausen and ONERA’s propulsion benches; programme-specific facilities such as the Ariane Group’s Vernon Test Centre and the BEAP booster bench in Kourou; industrial sites such as Avio and PLD Space; and newer facilities such as the UK National Space Propulsion Test Facility and the Łukasiewicz Rocket and Satellite Propulsion Laboratory Centre.

Founded in 1959, the DLR Institute of Space Propulsion (DLR Lampoldshausen) is one of Europe’s key research and testing hubs for liquid-chemical rocket engines. It brings together multiple departments covering the full chain of space propulsion work - from propellants and engine technology to testing - while also focusing on hydrogen-related technology transfer and the safe, efficient operation of rocket test stands and the supporting infrastructure, with strong emphasis on quality and safety

Ariane Group’s Vernon Test Centre PF52 is an ESA-owned cryogenic propulsion test facility located at Ariane Group’s site in Vernon, France. The Centre was historically used for LOX/LH2 engine subsystem development (including work supporting Vulcain/Vulcain 2) and subsequently upgraded with a dedicated Vinci test cell. Applied Hydrogen Technologies: The Applied Hydrogen Technologies department operates test facilities for hydrogen technologies and supports the development, testing and optimisation of hydrogen-based systems, components and complete systems. Its work links the Institute’s long-standing experience with liquid and gaseous hydrogen to the wider energy transition, including green hydrogen production, sector coupling and hydrogen infrastructure. The department also provides consulting, engineering, simulation and operational expertise for hydrogen-carrying systems, helping partners from research and industry bring hydrogen applications closer to market.57

Chemical Propellant Technology: The Chemical Propellant Technology department focuses on the development, characterization and testing of advanced propellants, propellant components, functional materials and new propulsion concepts. Its work is strongly driven by the search for alternatives to toxic conventional propellants such as hydrazine and NTO. The department carries out laboratory-scale synthesis, analytical characterization, compatibility and durability testing, ignition investigations and combustion tests, creating the early-stage scientific basis for future green propellant technologies.58

Engineering / Test Bench Technology: The Engineering department, listed under the Test Bench Technology page, provides the design and systems expertise needed to build and operate high-performance propulsion test benches. Its central role is to ensure that test stands can reproduce engine flight conditions as realistically as possible, supporting the principle “test as you fly – fly as you test.” The department’s capabilities include the conception, layout and development of test benches, altitude-simulation systems, upper-stage test capabilities, guide systems and steam-generator technologies.59

Quality and Product Assurance Management: The Quality and Product Assurance Management department ensures that test operations and space propulsion research meet the Institute’s quality, safety, environmental and legal requirements. It supports test campaigns throughout the project lifecycle, from development through test operation and maintenance. The department develops product assurance planning, monitors requirements implementation, supports risk assessments and root-cause analyses, maintains documented information and carries out internal audits to preserve high standards across the Institute.60

Rocket Engine Systems: The Rocket Engine Systems department develops and maintains systems expertise for liquid rocket propulsion. Its work covers the steady-state and transient behaviour of liquid rocket engines, the interaction of engine subcomponents and the control of full engine systems. The department addresses pressurised and pump-fed engines for main-stage, upper-stage, in-orbit and lander applications, with emphasis on cryogenic combinations such as liquid oxygen/liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen/hydrocarbon propellants, including liquid biomethane.61

Rocket Propulsion Technology: The Rocket Propulsion Technology department develops future cryogenic propulsion technologies through simulations, propulsion analyses and experimental testing. Its research ranges from fundamental combustion-chamber phenomena to application-oriented test conditions and component testing. Key activities include diagnostics for high-temperature and high-pressure thrust chambers, experimental work on reactive flows and nozzle acoustics, thermomechanical fatigue testing of chamber and nozzle structures, and investigations of injection, ignition and combustion instabilities.62

Spacecraft and Orbital Propulsion: The Spacecraft and Orbital Propulsion department investigates advanced propellants and propulsion types for satellite, orbital and aerospace applications. Its work supports the replacement of hydrazine-based systems with safer “green” alternatives, including ionic liquids, hydrogen peroxide / HTP, nitrous-oxide-based systems, gel propellants and hybrid propulsion concepts. The department operates the M11 research test stand, where engine tests are carried out at multiple positions to evaluate new propellants, propellant combinations and propulsion technologies.63

Safety and Hazard Prevention: The Safety and Hazard Prevention department safeguards operations at the Lampoldshausen site, where complex test and supply facilities operate under demanding safety requirements. It supports departments and facility operators in meeting safety standards and is responsible for safe test and facility operation, emergency management, fire protection, first aid, occupational health and safety, site security and environmental protection. The department also organises emergency and evacuation drills and maintains readiness for incidents at a site classified under Germany’s Hazardous Incident Ordinance.64

Test Facilities: The Test Facilities department operates the Institute’s large-scale propulsion test infrastructure at Lampoldshausen and carries out test campaigns for customers and partners. Its facilities support sea-level tests under ambient conditions as well as high-altitude simulation tests in vacuum. The department covers the full range of liquid chemical space propulsion testing, from component tests and engine tests to complete rocket-stage tests, including research and development, qualification and characterization campaigns across technology readiness levels.65

PF52 at ArianeGroup Vernon is used mainly for cryogenic Vinci upper-stage engine testing, covering hot-fire development, subsystem qualification, restart/re-ignition demonstrations, long-duration endurance firings, and production acceptance preparation. Its role complements high-altitude/vacuum testing at DLR Lampoldshausen: PF52 provides Vernon-based cryogenic engine test capability, including ambient-pressure operation with vacuum start-up conditions, while supporting the qualification and industrialisation of the Vinci engine for Ariane 6. Delving deeper into the types of testing conducted at the site, we see:

Cryogenic liquid rocket engine hot-fire testing: especially for the Vinci LOX/LH₂ upper-stage engine used on Ariane 6. PF52 is identified as the Vernon bench where Vinci qualification testing was completed.66

Vinci engine qualification testing: including formal qualification campaigns for the Ariane 6 upper-stage engine; ArianeGroup reported completion of the Vinci qualification campaign with the 148th test on PF52.67
Subsystem qualification testing: PF52 was used, alongside DLR’s P4.1 bench, for Vinci subsystem qualification campaigns M6 and M7.68

Restart / re-ignition testing: a major focus because Vinci is a re-ignitable upper-stage engine; tests included repeated “boosts,” including a campaign milestone of 20 successful boosts in one test.69

Long-duration firing and endurance testing: PF52-supported campaigns demonstrated extended operation, including a 1,569-second test, an 800-second continuous burn at maximum thrust, and a final qualification test lasting 957 seconds with two boosts.70

Acceptance-test preparation / production acceptance testing: an AIAA/EUCASS paper describes PF52’s future test cell as being designed for production acceptance tests, intended to shorten the acceptance process without reducing engine tuning quality or reliability contribution.71

Ambient-pressure engine testing with vacuum start-up conditions: the same source states that PF52 was planned to operate at ambient pressure, except during engine start-up, when it would operate under vacuum conditions.72
Development campaign testing: PF52 was intended for the last Vinci development test campaigns before qualification and production acceptance use.

Operating-domain and transient-behaviour testing: Vinci campaigns examined restart capability, accumulated firing time, operation at different points of the flight domain, start-up and shutdown robustness, and chill-down behaviour.73

Cryogenic component and subsystem testing at the broader Vernon test site: Vernon is described as a cryogenic propulsion site with multiple engine test stands and component-testing facilities, focused on LH₂/LOX propulsion for Ariane 5 and Ariane 6.74

The BEAP at the Guiana Space Centre is Europe’s dedicated full-scale solid-propellant booster test stand. It conducts static fire, development and qualification testing of large solid rocket motors for launch vehicles such as Ariane, Vega, Ariane 6, Vega-C and future Vega-E-related systems. Testing at BEAP validates motor performance, thrust, design, materials, manufacturing processes, nozzle actuation, safety systems and flight-representative behaviour under real operating conditions, with extensive instrumentation and post-fire data analysis supporting booster qualification and continuous improvement.75

Avio’s test facilities support the development and qualification of European launcher propulsion systems, with a strong focus on Vega-family solid rocket motors and next-generation liquid propulsion. At Sardinian facilities such as Salto di Quirra and the Space Propulsion Test Facility at Perdasdefogu, Avio conducts static firing, functional, qualification and requalification tests of solid motors such as Zefiro-40 and Zefiro-9, as well as hot-fire development tests of LOX–methane engines such as M10 for Vega E. These campaigns validate motor performance, nozzle behaviour, thrust-vector-control operation, burn duration, mixture-ratio control, throttling capability and flight-representative behaviour. Avio also contributes to testing of large common solid motors such as P120C and P160C for Ariane 6 and Vega-C/E, with full-scale qualification firings carried out at Europe’s Spaceport in French Guiana.

Solid rocket motor static firing tests: Full-scale motors are fired on the ground to validate thrust, pressure, burn time, structural behaviour and overall performance. Avio’s Zefiro motors for Vega and Vega-C have been tested at Sardinian test facilities, including Zefiro-40 and Zefiro-9 hot-fire campaigns.76

Development and qualification testing of Vega solid stages: Avio-built or Avio-led solid motors such as Zefiro-23, Zefiro-40 and Zefiro-9 have undergone qualification firings to prove flight readiness. ESA describes Zefiro-23 qualification at Salto di Quirra and Vega-C solid motor qualification campaigns including P120C, Zefiro-40 and Zefiro-9.77

Horizontal bench testing of Zefiro-40: Zefiro-40, the Vega-C second-stage solid motor, has been tested on a horizontal test bench at Avio’s Salto di Quirra facility. Recent testing included improved nozzle validation for Vega-C return-to-flight, with a scheduled 94-second burn simulating nominal in-flight performance.78

Nozzle design validation and requalification testing: Avio used Zefiro-40 firings to validate an improved nozzle assembly after Vega-C return-to-flight work. The first 2024 test was followed by a planned second firing to confirm data and qualify the revised second-stage motor configuration.79

Thrust-vector-control and manoeuvre simulation testing: Earlier Vega solid-motor qualification tests included large-amplitude thrust-vector-control movements to simulate demanding flight manoeuvres and verify control performance.80

Liquid rocket engine testing: Avio’s SPTF, Space Propulsion Test Facility, at Perdasdefogu / Salto di Quirra includes an LRE test bench for development and qualification testing of new-generation liquid rocket engines.81

LOX–methane / green cryogenic propulsion testing: The SPTF is specifically intended for low-environmental-impact engines using liquid oxygen and liquid methane, including the M10 / MR10-class engine for Vega E.82
M10 liquid oxygen–methane hot-fire testing: Avio has hot-fired the M10 engine at SPTF, including the first European successful test of a 10-tonne-thrust-class LOX–methane engine.83

Long-duration firing tests: M10 testing included cumulative burn-time campaigns, with Avio reporting 24 firings and 1,300 seconds cumulative firing in the first campaign, plus later long-duration testing.84

Throttling and mixture-ratio testing: Avio’s M10 DM2 campaign included high mixture-ratio testing, different thrust conditions, and a long-duration regulation/throttling test varying thrust and LOX–CH₄ mixture ratio during firing.85

Liquid oxygen turbopump technology testing: Avio develops and tests key technologies for liquid oxygen turbopumps, including the Dynamic Seal Package for the Vinci engine turbopump, which separates hot turbine gases from cryogenic liquid oxygen.86

Large common solid booster qualification testing: Avio is involved through Europropulsion in P120C/P160C solid motors for Ariane 6 and Vega. P120C qualification included development and qualification static firings, while P160C QM3 was hot-fired at BEAP in French Guiana in 2025 to support flight qualification.87

Nammo’s space-related testing is centred on propulsion systems and fluidic/mechanical components for in-space propulsion systems and launchers. Nammo states that the locations supporting its space test activities have extensive test benches and equipment for in-house qualification testing before customer delivery, with the Raufoss test facilities particularly dedicated to green propulsion using hydrogen peroxide. The listed space test capabilities include solid propulsion up to 100 kN, hybrid propulsion up to 200 kN, mono- and bipropellant thrusters, high-altitude facilities, and cleanroom/flow-bench infrastructure.88

For hybrid rocket propulsion testing, Nammo’s Raufoss facilities support engines such as the 30 kN hybrid engine used for the Nucleus sounding rocket. The engine is a green propulsion hybrid motor based on hydrogen peroxide technology, with 87.5% hydrogen peroxide and HTPB propellant, a 40-second thrust duration, pressure-regulated or blowdown operating modes, and possible restart capability. Nammo lists a 500 kN thrust test stand, multiple vibration test units, and a Hydrogen Peroxide Propulsion Test Facility at Raufoss.89

The site also conducts hybrid rocket motor static-fire testing under representative system conditions. ESA reported a Nammo final static firing in which the hybrid motor was connected to tanks, valves and piping on the test bench in a configuration representative of the flight setup. During the roughly 40-second burn, the motor generated 30 kN of thrust, equivalent to more than 40 kN in vacuum, supporting sounding-rocket and future small-launcher development.90

For sounding-rocket propulsion testing, Nammo’s Nucleus product line is directly space-related. Nammo states that the Nucleus sounding rocket is designed and manufactured at Raufoss and is intended to deliver experiments and spacecraft to high-altitude trajectories, with the maiden flight reaching 107 km. The Nucleus vehicle uses a 30 kN H₂O₂–HTPB hybrid propulsion unit with a 40-second burn time, making propulsion qualification and ground testing of this engine directly relevant to suborbital spaceflight.91

For monopropellant thruster and attitude-control testing, Nammo is developing and qualifying a 220 N hydrogen-peroxide monopropellant thruster for roll and attitude control systems. The thruster is intended for applications such as launcher roll and attitude control and stage-separation boost, including use on the Vega-C upper stage AVUM+. Nammo says it has expanded its green propulsion facilities to support development and manufacturing of H₂O₂-based attitude control systems, including a dedicated green-propellant test site and on-site hydrogen peroxide storage.92

For space-hardware vibration testing, Nammo’s Raufoss space product pages list multiple vibration test units as part of the site’s space-related test facilities. In this space context, those vibration units are relevant where they support qualification of propulsion hardware, thrusters, engines, components or sounding-rocket systems before delivery or flight use.93
ILOT Rocket and Satellite Propulsion Laboratory Centre

Łukasiewicz–ILOT’s Rocket and Satellite Propulsion Laboratory Centre is designed to support the development, qualification and testing of green rocket propulsion, satellite propulsion and other space technologies. Its infrastructure includes rocket-engine test stands for both atmospheric and vacuum conditions, satellite and corrective propulsion laboratories, rocket subsystem laboratories, chemical laboratories, environmental laboratories and composites facilities. The centre conducts rocket engine testing under atmospheric conditions for propulsion units up to 5 kN of thrust, as well as satellite propulsion testing under atmospheric conditions for units up to 20 N. These facilities are relevant for testing small rocket engines, satellite thrusters and corrective propulsion systems before higher-level integration or qualification.94

A key capability is vacuum space-propulsion testing, with continuous-vacuum test infrastructure for propulsion units up to 500 N of thrust. This supports qualification and development testing of propulsion systems under space-representative conditions, including small satellite engines, deorbiting propulsion and other in-space propulsion hardware. Łukasiewicz–ILOT also supports complete propulsion-system qualification and subsystem testing, including rocket and space subsystem laboratories for actuation and control systems, space avionics, flow components, valves and injectors. This means the centre can test not only engines and thrusters, but also the supporting hardware needed for integrated rocket and satellite propulsion systems. Additional specialist capabilities include rotating detonation engine testing for gaseous and liquid fuels, plus space-hardware environmental testing such as vibration, material, chemical, thermal and TVC chamber testing. For a concise report, these can be treated as supporting capabilities rather than the main headline test categories.95
SSC Esrange Space Center Testbed and Rocket Testing

SSC describes the Esrange Testbed as Europe’s first testing facility for reusable, sustainable and cost-effective rocket technology. Its services cover development, qualification and acceptance testing of rocket propulsion and flight hardware, ranging from engine-component testing through to flight tests of fully reusable launch vehicles.96 For rocket motor and engine testing, Esrange supports test firing of solid and liquid rocket motors in either vertical or horizontal positions. The facility is also used for engine and stage development tests, sustainable-propellant engine testing, and demonstrations of new components for space applications.97

For integrated stage and full-duration hot-fire testing, Esrange has hosted launcher-stage campaigns such as Rocket Factory Augsburg’s RFA ONE upper-stage integrated system test campaign. RFA reported a 280-second full-duration hot fire at Esrange, testing stage-level systems including fueling, fuel management, pressurization, sensors, propulsion and control.98

For reusable launcher testing, Esrange supports reusable sounding rocket motors, boosters and first-stage engines, including tethered tests, jump tests and controlled landings. The EU/ESA Themis programme is using Esrange for reusable-stage flight testing, with the first campaign focused on low-altitude hop testing, landing sequences and recovery-related operations.99

For commercial launch-vehicle engine testing, Isar Aerospace operates test facilities at Esrange for its Spectrum launch vehicle. SSC says these facilities support development tests, acceptance tests, qualification tests, full-duration engine firings, component-to-full-integration testing, and expanded integrated stage testing.100 For sounding rocket testing and flight campaigns, Esrange provides launch services for most types of sounding rockets and supports missions ranging from site-only launch use to full-service flight opportunities. SSC and its partners also support trajectory, load and stability analysis, structural design elements, service modules, telemetry and telecommand for research rocket missions.101

ONERA’s rocket-propulsion work includes solid, liquid and hybrid propellant testing through its Rocket Propulsion Laboratory, which ONERA says is focused on understanding physical phenomena in space and military thrusters and has installations for testing solid, liquid and hybrid propellants. ONERA’s Fauga-Mauzac site also has space propulsion test benches used for Ariane 6 first-stage work, where pressure and thrust measurements help validate future simulations.102 For cryogenic liquid rocket combustion, ONERA operates the MASCOTTE cryogenic test bench. Public ONERA material describes successful LOX/liquid-methane injector testing on MASCOTTE, including a double-swirl injector intended to improve propellant mixing for combustion. This makes MASCOTTE relevant for combustion, injector, propellant-mixing and diagnostic studies for liquid rocket engines.103

For electric satellite propulsion, ONERA’s ERIS installation is a vacuum test bench for electric propulsion. It reproduces the orbital satellite environment and enables performance and lifetime testing of electric/plasma thrusters under sustained vacuum conditions, including xenon pumping and cryogenic trapping to preserve test quality during long campaigns.104 Finally, ONERA also supports launcher propulsion-integration testing through wind-tunnel and propulsion-simulation capabilities. Its launcher test services include complete models or components, booster separation simulation, hot and cold jet simulation, nozzle testing and testing across different flight phases such as separation, cruise, high-angle-of-attack and limit-envelope conditions.105

PLD Space’s propulsion test facilities are located at Teruel Airport in Spain and are used for testing and qualifying the company’s liquid-fuel rocket engines and launcher hardware. Teruel Airport describes the site as a liquid-fuel rocket-engine test bench where motors are integrated for safe static firing, originally supporting the qualification of PLD Space’s suborbital vehicle engines.106 The main activity is liquid rocket engine static-fire and qualification testing, covering PLD Space’s TEPREL engine family for MIURA launch vehicles. PLD’s MIURA 1 qualification work included complete rocket static testing, combined qualification tests and hot-fire tests; GMV describes the campaign as including functional validation plus three static-fire tests of 5, 20 and 110 seconds, with the longest acting as a full mission test on the ground.107

For MIURA 5, PLD Space’s Teruel infrastructure has expanded into a broader launcher test site. Recent reporting based on PLD Space material describes more than 155,000 m² of facilities with 10 test benches for validating MIURA 5 subsystems, including engines, combustion chambers, turbopumps, gas generators, tanks, the complete second stage, stage separation systems, and valves.108 The facilities also support integrated propulsion hardware testing, especially for the TEPREL-C engine. PLD Space reported completing integrated testing of the main TEPREL-C hardware ahead of the engine’s flight-qualification campaign, while related sources identify combustion chambers, turbopumps and gas generators as key hardware being tested for MIURA 5.109

At vehicle level, PLD Space uses the facilities for stage and launcher system validation, including wet dress rehearsal-style testing, full-stage feed-system behaviour, structural validation of tanks, and testing of stage-separation, valve and umbilical systems. For the MIURA 5 qualification unit, PLD Space states that the first stage will undergo a wet dress rehearsal to validate full feed-system behaviour, while other qualification work covers engines, avionics, interstage and fairing systems.110

Several high-level observations emerge from the data included in the table above. The network of testing centres is highly diverse in both geography and function, with facilities spread across major European space-faring states and supporting everything from laboratory analysis to full-duration static firings and operational launch support. Third, the data suggests a mixed institutional model where some centres are publicly owned and research oriented, others are closely ties to specific industrial actors or launcher programmes, whilst others combine both public and private roles. Finally, there is evidence of transition within the testing centre sector, with newer facilities and test programmes placing greater emphasis on reusability, open-access testing, and more sustainable or “green” propulsion technologies, as demonstrated by the testing conducted at ILOT and Esrange. Space Situational Awareness Facilities

Space Situational Awareness (SSA) Facilities are key to supporting European operations and activities to, in and from space. All examined facilities were operated by public actors, typically from institutional or research centres. These facilities are vital in support launch missions by assessing and investigating space objects to support collision avoidance, fragmentation, as well as space weather events and potential near-Earth objects (NEO). The EU SST Partnership in particular is a collaborative framework under the EU Space Programme that supports SSA through a distributed network of facilities across 19 EU Member States. EU SST does not currently provide LCOLA but contribution to EU SST is still included in the table below, because it is indicative of the sharing of collision avoidance data amongst Member States.

The SSA Space Weather Coordination Centre (SSCC) at the Space Pole in Belgium operates Europe’s first Space Weather Helpdesk, answering questions about the SSA service network, its products, and space weather conditions.

In its own words the office "provides 24/7 forecasts and warnings of space weather for Government and responder communities, critical national infrastructure providers and the public and will continue to develop its forecast capability."

Koninklijk Nederlands Meteorologisch Instituut conducts space weather research supporting SSA monitoring, modeling, forecasting. The R&D Satellite Observations department handles space weather-related research.

The Istituto Nazionale di Geofisica e Vulcanologia studies geomagnetism and ionosphere supporting SSA monitoring.

The EU SST Collision Avoidance service provides spacecraft operators with collision-risk assessment and alerts to help protect satellites and maintain safe operations in orbit.

Europe’s access to space depends on highly specialised transportation networks that link geographically dispersed manufacturing centres, ports, test sites, and spaceports. The infrastructure examined here illustrates that space logistics in Europe is built around the movement of oversized and high-value components that cannot be handled through standard freight systems. Instead, the sector relies on dedicated marine assets such as Canopée, the MN Toucan, and the MN Colibri for regular transatlantic transport to Korou; specialised transport containers for launcher stages; and heavy-lift aircraft such as the Antonov An-124 and Airbus BelugaXL for particularly large cargo, such as launch components. Simultaneously, Rocket Factory Augsburg’s tank deliveries to SaxaVord Spaceport also illustrate the importance of smaller scale, multi-modal logistics chains in supporting emerging launch sites within Europe’s periphery.
Table 8 Mapping of critical ground infrastructure – Transportation

Canopée is a 121 m-long, sail-assisted hybrid cargo ship purpose-built for ArianeGroup/ESA logistics to transport Ariane 6 stages and sub-assemblies from European ports (Bremen–Rotterdam–Le Havre–Bordeaux) across the Atlantic to Pariacabo/Kourou in French Guiana (Europe’s spaceport). Equipped with four fully automated, 37 m-high OceanWings that rotate to follow the wind, it can carry ~5,000 tonnes and is designed to cut average fuel use/emissions by ~30% versus conventional propulsion. Canopée was also used to deliver the hardware for the inaugural Ariane 64 launch, which orbited 32 Amazon LEO satellites in February 2026.
ArianeGroup · ESA · CNES/Europe's Spaceport (CSG) · Amazon Leo

Ariane 6 transport containers are large, specialized structures designed to safely store and transport rocket stages between European production facilities and the launch site. Developed by APCO Technologies with ArianeGroup, they protect sensitive components from mechanical stress, contamination, and environmental conditions. The containers maintain a secure internal mounting system so stages remain stable during road, river, and sea transport. A typical container for the Ariane 6 upper stage measures about 14 m × 7 m × 6 m, reflecting the size of the launcher components

Built in 1995, MN Toucan is a special-purpose roll on/roll off (Ro-Ro) and lift-on/lift-off (Lo-Lo) cargo vessel purpose-built to transport Ariane launcher components from Europe to Kourou/Pariacabo (French Guiana) for Arianespace launch campaigns. It was also used for Soyuz-component transport, but this has since been suspended

Built in 2000, MN Colibri is a roll on/roll of (Ro-Ro) cargo vessel and specially designed for space logistics, having carried Ariane 5 and Soyuz launcher components from Europe to French Guiana (Kourou/Pariacabo) under long-term charter arrangements
Arianespace · Rostic’s Progress Rocket Space Centre · ASI/Avio (Vega)

Airbus BelugaXL is a large cargo aircraft operated by Airbus to transport oversized components between European aerospace production sites. Based on the Airbus A330, it replaces the earlier Airbus A300-600ST Beluga fleet and provides significantly increased cargo volume for large structures. Its distinctive enlarged fuselage allows the transport of aircraft sections, satellites, and other bulky aerospace hardware

Antonov An-124 heavy cargo aircraft are chartered by ESA and European space companies to transport large spacecraft, satellites, and launch hardware between manufacturing, testing, and launch sites. The aircraft’s oversized cargo hold, nose-opening door, and internal cranes allow the loading of large transport containers and delicate space components. With a payload capacity of around 120 tonnes, it is one of the few aircraft capable of carrying complete satellite assemblies or rocket elements
Rocket Factory Augsburg Transport Storage Tanks

To support the transport of four 18m long x 4m diameter steel water storage tanks from Aberdeen to Baltasound, Shetland, for the SaxaVord Spaceport. Ocean Kinetics deployed their barge P7 and Multicat BK Marjorie to carry out the 50+ mile sea transport. Working with DFDS, the tanks were loaded onto the Ocean Kinetics barge in Lerwick and transported by sea to Baltasound Harbour. There, they were offloaded by RS Henderson and transported to the spaceport in Unst.

A few high-level observations emerge from the table above. Most notably, maritime transport appears to be the backbone of European space transportation logistics, particularly for the Ariane programme and the Europe-French Guiana corridor. Furthermore, much of this transportation infrastructure is purpose-built or heavily adapted to the sheer size and sensitivity of space hardware, highlighting the extent to which this transportation infrastructure itself comprises an important part of Europe’s access to space.

Operations centres comprise a core layer of Europe’s access to space infrastructure, as they provide the command, control, and coordination functions that allow launches, The facilities identified here illustrate that Europe’s operational architecture covers the full mission cycle: launch control through the Jupiter Control Room; spacecraft operations and flight dynamics through centres such as ESA’s ESOC and DLR’s GSOC; Earth observation data handling at ESRIN; human spaceflight support through the Columbus Control Centre; and service-specific constellation management through the Galileo and EUMETSAT control centres. Take together, these sites demonstrate that European access to space depends on a dense and highly-specialised network of centres that sustain missions in orbit, manage the flow of data, and ensure continuity of critical services.
Table 9 Mapping of critical ground infrastructure – Operations centres

The Jupiter Control Room (also called Mission Control Jupiter) is the primary operations centre at Europe’s Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, responsible for real-time monitoring, control, and coordination of launcher countdowns and flight operations. Managed jointly by CNES and ESA, Jupiter integrates telemetry, tracking, and command systems to support Ariane, Vega, and Soyuz launch campaigns, providing launch-vehicle status, safety oversight, and mission sequencing from final T-0 through flight

ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) is responsible for operating ESA’s fleet of satellites and deep-space missions. Its primary function is the operation of uncrewed spacecraft on behalf of ESA and the launch and early orbit phases of ESA and third-party missions. ESOC provides mission planning, flight dynamics, telemetry/telecommand, and spacecraft navigation across a wide range of missions (Earth observation, science, exploration, telecommunications). It manages communications via ESA’s ESTRACK ground station network and is evolving toward next-generation operations infrastructure to support future complex missions.
No single LV; it takes over spacecraft just after lift-off for LEOP

European Space Research Institute (ESRIN) is an Earth observation data operations centre of the European Space Agency located in Frascati. It manages the processing, archiving, and distribution of satellite data from ESA Earth observation missions. ESRIN operates major ground-segment infrastructure and data hubs supporting programmes such as the Copernicus Programme and missions like the Sentinel missions
No single LV, but mainly associated with Vega/Vega-C

German Space Operations Center (GSOC) is the primary mission operations centre of the German Aerospace Center (DLR). It is responsible for planning, monitoring, and controlling national and international space missions, including scientific, Earth observation, navigation, and human spaceflight missions. GSOC operates satellite control systems and communication infrastructure that support spacecraft operations from launch through routine mission phases. The centre has supported more than five decades of missions and forms a key part of Germany’s spaceflight operations capability
No single LV; GSOC is a multi-mission spacecraft operations centre covering LEOP, commissioning, routine operations, satellite missions, and human-spaceflight support

Columbus Control Centre is a human spaceflight operations centre operated by the German Aerospace Center (DLR) on behalf of the European Space Agency at the German Space Operations Center (GSOC) in Germany. The centre commands and monitors the systems of the Columbus laboratory and coordinates European scientific experiments conducted on board the International Space Station. It operates continuously, providing communications, payload coordination, and operational support for astronauts working in the European laboratory
No single LV; provides human-spaceflight communications and operations support for ESA astronauts and Columbus/ISS activities

EUMETSAT Mission Control Centres (MCC) are the satellite operations and control facilities of the EUMETSAT, located at its headquarters in Darmstadt. The centres are responsible for the safe operation of EUMETSAT’s meteorological satellites, providing continuous monitoring, command, and control of spacecraft and their ground infrastructure. They ensure communication with satellites and the acquisition of environmental data through a network of ground stations across Europe. Separate control rooms support both geostationary and low-Earth-orbit missions, as well as Copernicus satellites such as Sentinel-3 and Sentinel-6
No single LV; LVs vary by missions; for example, Metop-SGA1 launched on Ariane 62 in August 2025, then EUMETSAT took control after LEOP

Galileo Control Centres (GCC) are the main navigation system operations centres for Europe’s Galileo. Two centres are located in Oberpfaffenhofen and Fucino, forming the core of the Galileo ground segment. They monitor and control the Galileo satellite constellation, manage navigation data and timing, and ensure the accuracy and reliability of the positioning signals broadcast to users worldwide. The centres operate in a redundant configuration so that one can take over operations if the other becomes unavailable
DLR Gesellschaft für Raumfahrtanwendungen (DLR GfR) · Telespazio · · (Operational oversight by EUSPA)
No single LV; Galileo spacecraft have used Soyuz, Ariane 5, Falcon 9, and Ariane 6

Galileo Security Monitoring Centre (GSMC) is part of the ground segment of the Galileo and is operated by the European Union Agency for the Space Programme. The centres monitor the security and operational status of the Galileo system and respond to security or cyber-security threats that could affect service availability. They also manage access to the secure Public Regulated Service (PRS) used by authorised government users. The GSMC operates from two sites—Saint-Germain-en-Laye (main site) and San Martín de la Vega (backup)—ensuring continuous monitoring and resilience of the Galileo infrastructure
Saint-Germain-en-Laye, France · San Martín de la Vega, Spain
N/A; GSMC is a Galileo security ops centre monitoring security/cyber threats and Galileo component status
CNES Centre spatial de Toulouse (Toulouse Space Centre)

Toulouse Space Centre is the main technical and operations centre of the Centre National d'Études Spatiales (CNES). The centre is responsible for the design, development, and operation of satellite systems and associated ground infrastructure. It hosts mission control facilities used for satellite operations, orbital control, and the management of space data

A few high-level observations emerge from the table above. First, Europe’s operations centre landscape is highly functionally differentiated. Notably, different centres are responsible for launcher operations, satellite command and control, navigation services, meteorology, Earth observation, human spaceflight, and system security. Second, the network of operations centres is geographically distributed across multiple European states, indicating that operational capacity is shared across national and inter-governmental institutions rather than concentrated in a single location. Third, resilience appears baked into this network, especially within systems such as Galileo, where redundant control and security centres help ensure continuity in the event of technical failure or disruption. Finally, the data suggests that Europe’s operational infrastructure is closely tied to the continent’s broader strategic objectives, as it supports autonomous navigation, weather services, and environmental monitoring in additional to supporting launch and spacecraft management.
euProviders: This subsection analyses the contribution of launch service providers currently expected to generate demand for EU and ESA launch infrastructure over the 2025 to 2035 period. The analysis focuses on providers with confirmed or credible plans to operate from launch facilities located in EU Member States or ESA Member States, as identified in Chapter 3.

For each provider, publicly available information on vehicle development status, entry into service timelines and indicative launch cadence is used to derive a realistic contribution to infrastructure demand. Provider level data is used strictly as an analytical input. Where providers operate or plan to operate from both European and non-European spaceports, only the portion of activity expected to take place from EU and ESA launch facilities is retained.
Arianespace / ArianeGroup (Ariane 6)
Arianespace has publicly indicated a near-term ramp-up to around 6–8 Ariane 6 missions in 2026, representing a significant increase compared to 2025.

In the medium term, Arianespace has explored the possibility of going beyond approximately 10 launches per year, suggesting that this level should be considered a baseline target rather than a strict upper limit.

In terms of forecast implications, Ariane 6 represents the most credible pathway toward achieving a stable cadence of around 10 launches per year in the late 2020s, provided that industrial production stabilises and sufficient institutional and commercial demand materialises.
Avio (Vega C / Vega E transition)
ESA has signed contracts explicitly aimed at increasing the annual flight rate of Vega-C while supporting the development of Vega-E.
Current reporting indicates that Vega-C is expected to remain operational until approximately 2031, with Block upgrades foreseen around 2028, although these timelines remain subject to change.

In terms of forecast implications, Vega’s launch cadence is expected to peak in the late 2020s, after which it will become dependent on the transition to Vega-E and on continued institutional demand planning.
Isar Aerospace (Spectrum)
Isar Aerospace is continuing efforts toward a second flight and qualification campaign in 2026, with schedule volatility remaining typical for early-stage launch systems.

In terms of forecast implications, once orbital capability is achieved, launch cadence may increase progressively; however, the initial operational phase is expected to remain limited to 1–3 launches per year, before higher cadence can be supported through operational maturity and customer confidence.
Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA ONE)
RFA has stated that its first orbital launch is currently planned for summer 2026.
Following a successful first flight, the company has indicated that it expects to reach an initial cadence of up to around 4 launches per year within the subsequent two years.

In terms of forecast implications, a realistic ramp-up would consist of one launch in 2026, increasing to approximately 2–4 launches per year by 2028, followed by gradual scaling as infrastructure and operations mature.
PLD Space (Miura 5)
PLD Space positions Miura 5 as a high-frequency launch service, with corporate communication referring to around 30 launch slots per year.
Independent reporting indicates that the company has set an ambition to reach more than 30 launches per year by 2030, although this should be considered a high-end scenario.
The first orbital launch is still framed around 2026.

In terms of forecast implications, while PLD is one of the few European startups explicitly targeting high cadence, the base-case scenario assumes a more gradual ramp-up, as multi-site operations and industrial scaling require time.
MaiaSpace (Maia - owned by ArianeGroup)
MaiaSpace has publicly postponed its inaugural flight to 2027.
Market reporting indicates an ambition to reach up to around 20 launches per year in the early 2030s, with early demand partly linked to constellation operators such as OneWeb.

In terms of forecast implications, despite strong industrial backing, reusable launch systems typically require several flights to reach maturity, suggesting a gradual ramp toward high single-digit launches per year by 2030.
Skyrora (Skyrora XL)
Current reporting indicates that the Skyrora XL demonstrator timeline has shifted to early 2027.
The regulatory framework allows for up to 16 launches per year from SaxaVord, although this represents a licensing ceiling rather than an expected operational level.
In terms of forecast implications, the most likely scenario remains a limited cadence of a few launches per year, unless supported by strong institutional anchor demand.
HyImpulse (SL1)
HyImpulse indicates a target of up to 12 launches per year, alongside a longer-term aspiration of reaching 50 launches per year by 2030, which should be considered highly aspirational.
Independent reporting places the expected orbital debut of SL1 around 2027.

In terms of forecast implications, while hybrid propulsion offers differentiation, actual launch cadence will remain constrained by vehicle qualification, launch site availability, and market demand, resulting in a base case significantly below the stated ambitions.
Latitude (Zéphyr)
Latitude is targeting a first launch in 2026, with development timelines indicating a launch within approximately 18 months from early 2026.
The company is also developing a manufacturing facility capable of producing up to around 50 rockets per year, although this reflects production capacity rather than achievable launch cadence.
In terms of forecast implications, while manufacturing capacity may scale rapidly, actual launch cadence will remain constrained by spaceport availability, market demand and operational maturity.
HyPrSpace (OB‑1 / Orbital Baguette One)

HyPrSpace is developing OB‑1, an orbital microlauncher with a stated payload capacity of around 250 kg to low Earth orbit, following a suborbital demonstrator, Baguette One, planned for launch in 2026 from mainland France.

The company has publicly indicated an ambition to attempt a first orbital launch by the end of 2027. It has also outlined a longer-term industrial concept sized around a production facility capable of supporting up to approximately eight orbital launchers per year, although this remains an aspirational long-term target rather than an operationally demonstrated cadence.

Forecast implication: HyPrSpace is a credible emerging French microlauncher actor and should be monitored as a potential source of future demand for European launch infrastructure. However, because the orbital launch site for OB‑1 has not yet been publicly confirmed, its contribution should be treated cautiously in the base case and can be reflected instead in a sensitivity scenario until site allocation and launch licensing become clearer.

Non-EU/ESA launch providers
The possibility that non-European launch vehicles could generate demand for European infrastructure was explicitly reviewed.

Soyuz operations from the Guiana Space Centre were suspended in 2022 following geopolitical developments and the termination of cooperation agreements. There are no credible signals indicating a resumption of Soyuz launches from European territory within the 2025 to 2035 timeframe. Soyuz is therefore excluded from the forecast.

At present, no US commercial heavy or medium launch providers, including SpaceX, Blue Origin or United Launch Alliance, have announced or negotiated plans to operate orbital launches from EU or ESA launch sites. Their operational models remain fully anchored to US launch ranges, and no European infrastructure adaptation programmes have been initiated for their vehicles. As a result, these providers are excluded from the demand forecast.
Similarly, Chinese launch systems are excluded, both because of regulatory constraints and the absence of any cooperation framework that would enable the use of European launch infrastructure.

Other emerging non-European commercial launch providers, including from Asia or the Middle East, were screened. There is no evidence of non-European launch vehicles planning to operate from European territory during the forecast period.
As a result of this screening, the demand forecast reflects:
All launches expected to take place from EU and ESA launch facilities by European launch service providers
No launches by non European providers, given the absence of credible plans to use European infrastructure over the period considered
While the methodology remains open to the inclusion of non-European providers should future policies enable such use, no such scenarios are currently identifiable on an evidence‑based basis.
